questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds, its displacement is \(x\) metres from the origin \(O\). Its velocity is given by \(v = 2-4\cos 2t\), for \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\).

parts.stem: (a) Find the initial velocity of the particle.
parts.hint: The initial velocity is \(v\) at \(t=0\).

steps.explain: Substitute \(t=0\) into the velocity function.
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (b) Find all the times when the particle is at rest, where \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\).
parts.hint: At rest means \(v=0\). Solve \(2-4\cos 2t = 0\), being careful with the doubled domain for the angle \(2t\).

steps.explain: Set the velocity to zero and isolate \(\cos 2t\).
Since \(0\le t\le 2\pi\), the angle \(2t\) ranges over \(0 \le 2t \le 4\pi\) — two full revolutions. List all solutions for \(2t\) where cosine equals \(\tfrac12\) in that extended range.
Divide every solution by 2 to get \(t\).

parts.stem: (c) Sketch the graph of \(v\) as a function of \(t\), showing all key features.

steps.explain: Mark the key features already found: initial value \(v=-2\) at \(t=0\), and the four rest times (\(v=0\)) from part (b).
The function oscillates between a minimum of \(v=2-4=-2\) and a maximum of \(v=2+4=6\), completing one full cosine cycle every \(\pi\) seconds (since the angle is \(2t\)).
Sketch the full curve over \(0\le t\le 2\pi\), matching the graph shown above.
steps.work: Curve as shown, with maxima at \(t=\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}\) (\(v=6\)) and minima at \(t=0, \pi, 2\pi\) (\(v=-2\)).

parts.stem: (d) Find the acceleration of the particle when \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
parts.hint: Acceleration is \(\ddot{x} = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\). Differentiate \(v\), then substitute \(t=\pi/2\) — or note that \(t=\pi/2\) is a turning point of \(v\) on the graph in part (c).

steps.explain: Differentiate the velocity function to get acceleration.
Substitute \(t=\pi/2\).
Evaluate — this matches the graph in part (c), where \(t=\pi/2\) is a maximum turning point of \(v\) (so its gradient, the acceleration, is momentarily zero).

parts.stem: (e) Find the exact displacement of the particle when \(t=\pi\), given that its initial displacement is 3 metres to the right of the origin.
parts.hint: Integrate \(v\) to find \(x\) (with a constant \(C\)), use \(x(0)=3\) to find \(C\), then substitute \(t=\pi\).

steps.explain: Integrate the velocity function to find displacement, including the constant of integration.
Use the initial condition \(x(0)=3\) to find \(C\).
Substitute \(t=\pi\) into the full displacement equation.
Simplify.
steps.work: \(x = 2\pi+3\) metres to the right of the origin.

questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line. At time \( t \) seconds, its distance \( x \) metres from a fixed point \( O \) is given by \( x=1-\cos2t \), for \( 0\le t\le\pi \).

parts.stem: (a) Sketch the graph of \( x \) as a function of \( t \) for \( 0\le t\le\pi \).
parts.answer: A cosine-shaped curve: starts at \( (0,0) \), rises to a maximum \( (\tfrac{\pi}{2},2) \), then falls back to \( (\pi,0) \).

steps.explain: Step 1: Identify the key features of the trigonometric function \( x = 1 - \cos(2t) \). The principal axis (centre line) is at \( x=1 \). The amplitude is 1. The period is \( \dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi \).
Step 2: Find the key coordinates (start, quarter, half, three-quarters, and end of the period) by substituting \( t = 0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \pi \).
steps.work: t=0 \implies x=0 \\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \implies x=1 \\ t=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \implies x=2 \\ t=\dfrac{3\pi}{4} \implies x=1 \\ t=\pi \implies x=0

steps.explain: Step 3: Plot these key points on a Cartesian plane and draw a smooth, continuous wave (an inverted cosine shape) passing through them.

parts.stem: (b) At what times is the particle at rest, and what is its position at those times?

steps.explain: The particle is at rest when its velocity is zero. Differentiate \( x \) with respect to \( t \) to find the velocity.
Set the velocity to zero and solve for \( t \) in \( 0\le t\le\pi \) (so \( 2t\in[0,2\pi] \)).
Substitute each value of \( t \) back into \( x=1-\cos2t \) to find the corresponding position.

parts.stem: (c) Find the velocity of the particle when \( t=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \).

steps.explain: Using the velocity function \( v=2\sin2t \) found in part (a), substitute \( t=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
Evaluate \( \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1 \).

parts.stem: (d) For what values of \( t\in[0,\pi] \) is the particle’s velocity greater than 1 m/s?

steps.explain: Set up the inequality using \( v=2\sin2t \).

Divide every part of the inequality by 2 to solve for \( t \).

Distance is the sum of the absolute values of each displacement (since the particle reverses direction at t=1, one interval's displacement is negative). Pitfall: adding the signed displacements directly (instead of absolute values) understates the true distance travelled.

parts.stem: (a) Sketch the graph of \(x\) as a function of \(t\) for \(0 \le t \le \pi\).

steps.explain: This is a cosine curve, reflected (due to the \(-\cos\)) and shifted up by 1. The amplitude is 1, midline is \(x=1\), and since the angle is \(2t\), the period is \(\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi\).
Plot the key points: \(x(0)=1-\cos0=0\); \(x(\pi/2)=1-\cos\pi=2\) (maximum); \(x(\pi)=1-\cos2\pi=0\).
Sketch the smooth curve through these points, as shown above.
steps.work: Curve rises from \((0,0)\) to peak \((\pi/2,2)\), then falls back to \((\pi,0)\).

parts.stem: (b) Using your graph, or otherwise, find the times when the particle is at rest and the position of the particle at each of these times. Which of the following is correct?

steps.explain: The particle is at rest when its velocity \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0\) — on the graph, this is where the curve has a turning point (horizontal tangent).
Within \(0\le t\le\pi\), solve for \(t\) — these match the turning points visible on the graph in part (a): the start, the peak, and the end.
Read the corresponding \(x\)-position at each of these times directly from the graph (or the original equation).

parts.stem: (c) Find the velocity of the particle when \(t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
parts.hint: Differentiate \(x\) to get \(v\), then substitute \(t=\pi/4\).

steps.explain: Differentiate \(x=1-\cos2t\) to find the velocity function.
Substitute \(t=\pi/4\).
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (d) When is the particle's velocity greater than \(1\text{ m/s}\) (for \(0 \le t \le \pi\))?
parts.hint: Solve \(2\sin 2t = 1\) first to find the critical values, then use the graph of \(v\) to see between which two times \(v>1\).

steps.explain: Find where \(v=1\) exactly, since these are the boundary (critical) values of the inequality.
Solve for \(2t\), then \(t\), within the extended range \(0 \le 2t \le 2\pi\).

Since \(v=2\sin2t\) rises from 0, peaks, then falls, it exceeds 1 only *between* these two critical times (not outside them) — this can be confirmed by testing a value like \(t=\pi/4\) from part (c), where \(v=2>1\), and \(\pi/4\) lies between \(\pi/12\) and \(5\pi/12\).
State the solution interval.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis. At a certain time, \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-2\text{ ms}^{-2}\) and \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1\text{ ms}^{-1}\). Which statement describes the motion of the particle at that time?
options: The particle is moving to the right with increasing speed.
The particle is moving to the left with decreasing speed.
The particle is moving to the right with decreasing speed.
The particle is moving to the left with increasing speed.
questions.hint: The sign of velocity gives the direction; when velocity and acceleration have opposite signs, the particle is slowing down (decelerating).

steps.explain: Velocity \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1>0\), so the particle is moving in the positive direction — to the right.
Acceleration \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-2<0\) is in the opposite direction to the velocity. When acceleration opposes velocity, the particle is decelerating (its speed is decreasing).
steps.work: Acceleration and velocity have opposite signs \(\;\Rightarrow\;\) speed decreasing

steps.explain: Combine both facts.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) moving to the right with decreasing speed

questions.stem: The graph shows the displacement x of a particle moving along a straight line as a function of time t. Which statement describes the motion of the particle at the point P?
options: The velocity is negative and the acceleration is positive.
The velocity is negative and the acceleration is negative.
The velocity is positive and the acceleration is positive.
The velocity is positive and the acceleration is negative.
questions.hint: On a displacement-time graph, the tangent slope gives velocity. The way that slope changes gives acceleration.

steps.explain: At \(P\) the displacement curve slopes downward (red tangent), so the gradient \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) is negative: the velocity is negative.
Near \(P\) the curve bends upward (concave up): the tangent slope is increasing (orange, then green tangents), so \(\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}>0\) and the acceleration is positive.
Therefore the particle has negative velocity and positive acceleration.

questions.stem: The velocity of a particle moving along the \(x\)-axis is given by \(v=8-8e^{-2t}\), where \(t\) is the time in seconds and \(x\) is the displacement in metres.

parts.stem: Show that the particle is initially at rest.
parts.hint: Substitute \(t=0\) into the given velocity function.

steps.explain: The velocity is given directly as \(v(t)=8-8e^{-2t}\). Its graph starts at the origin.
At the initial instant \(t=0\), \(e^0=1\).
Zero velocity means the particle is initially at rest.

parts.stem: Show that the acceleration of the particle is always positive.
parts.hint: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Remember the chain-rule factor when differentiating \(e^{-2t}\).

steps.explain: Differentiate \(v(t)=8-8e^{-2t}\).
An exponential is positive for every real \(t\), and \(16\) is positive.
Therefore acceleration is positive for all t.

parts.stem: Explain why the particle is moving in the positive direction for all \(t>0\).
parts.hint: Factor the velocity and compare \(e^{-2t}\) with \(1\) for positive \(t\).

steps.explain: Factor the given velocity. The graph stays above the \(t\)-axis for \(t>0\).
Thus \(1-e^{-2t}>0\), and multiplying by \(8\) keeps it positive. Positive velocity means positive direction.

parts.stem: As \(t\to\infty\), the velocity of the particle approaches a constant. Find the value of this constant.
parts.hint: As \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-2t}\) tends to zero.

steps.explain: Use \(v(t)=8-8e^{-2t}\). The dashed line shows the value the velocity approaches.
As t becomes large, the exponential term tends to zero.
The velocity therefore tends to 8.

parts.stem: Sketch the graph of the particle’s velocity as a function of time.
parts.answer: An increasing, concave-down curve starting at \((0,0)\) and approaching the horizontal asymptote \(v=8\).
parts.hint: Use the initial velocity, positive acceleration, and limiting velocity. The acceleration decreases toward zero, so the \(v(t)\) curve flattens.

steps.explain: At \(t=0\), \(v=0\), so mark the origin. The initial slope is \(a(0)=16\).
Since acceleration is positive, velocity increases. Since \(a(t)=16e^{-2t}\) decreases toward zero, the slope of the velocity graph gets smaller.
As \(t\to\infty\), \(v\to8\), so draw a horizontal asymptote at \(v=8\).

questions.stem: The graph shows the velocity of a particle, \(v\) metres per second, as a function of time, \(t\) seconds.

parts.stem: What is the initial velocity of the particle?
parts.hint: Read the velocity graph at \(t=0\).

steps.explain: Initial time is \(t=0\). Locate where the curve meets the vertical axis.
So the initial velocity is \(20\) metres per second.

parts.stem: When is the velocity of the particle equal to zero?
parts.hint: Velocity is zero where the graph crosses the horizontal time axis.

steps.explain: Find the point where the velocity curve crosses \(v=0\).
The graph crosses the axis at \(t=10\).

parts.stem: When is the acceleration of the particle equal to zero?
parts.hint: Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph. It is zero where that graph has a horizontal tangent.

steps.explain: Acceleration is \(\frac{dv}{dt}\), so it is the slope of the velocity graph: positive where \(v\) rises (green), negative where it falls (red).
The velocity graph has a horizontal tangent at its maximum, at \(t=6\).
Therefore acceleration is zero at \(6\) seconds.

questions.stem: A particle is moving along a straight line with displacement \(x\) at time \(t\). The particle is stationary when \(t=11\) and when \(t=13\). Which of the following MUST be true?
options: The particle changes direction at some time between \(t=11\) and \(t=13\).
The displacement function has a stationary point at some time between \(t=11\) and \(t=13\).
The acceleration is zero at some time between \(t=11\) and \(t=13\).
The acceleration function has a stationary point at some time between \(t=11\) and \(t=13\).
questions.hint: Consider the velocity at the two times, then apply Rolle’s theorem to the velocity function between them.

steps.explain: “Stationary” means the velocity is zero at both stated times.
The velocity has equal values at the ends of this interval. Since it is differentiable, Rolle’s theorem says its derivative is zero somewhere between 11 and 13.
The derivative of velocity is acceleration. So the acceleration must be zero at some time in the interval.

questions.stem: At time \(t\) a particle has displacement and acceleration functions \(x(t)\) and \(a(t)\). For which of the following functions is \(x(t)\equiv a(t)\)?
questions.hint: Acceleration is the SECOND derivative of displacement: \(a(t)=x''(t)\). Differentiate each option twice and see which gives back the original function.

steps.explain: Acceleration.
Option A: \(x=3\sin t-e^t\).
Option B: \(x=3\cos t-e^{-t}\).
Option C: \(x=e^t-e^{-t}\).
Option D: \(x=3\sin t-3\cos t\).
steps.work: \(x'=3\cos t+3\sin t,\quad x''=-3\sin t+3\cos t\ne x\) ✗

steps.explain: Only C satisfies \(x''=x\).

keyPoints.text: acceleration functions
keyPoints.note: Differentiate twice; compare with the original.

questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line. At time \(t\) seconds, its displacement from the origin is \(x\) metres and is given by \(x=1-\cos2t\). Using your graph, or otherwise, find the times when the particle is at rest and the position of the particle at these times.
questions.hint: At rest means the VELOCITY is zero: \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0\). On the graph that is where the tangent is horizontal (turning points) — including the end points of the interval.

steps.explain: Velocity.
At rest: \(v=0\).
In \(0\le t\le\pi\) we have \(0\le2t\le2\pi\), where sine is zero at \(0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi\).
Positions: substitute into \(x=1-\cos2t\).

keyPoints.note: At rest means velocity zero; solve sine equal to zero.

questions.stem: The graph shows the velocity \(v\) of a particle moving along a straight line as a function of time \(t\). Taking the rightward direction as positive, which statement describes the motion of the particle at the point \(P\)?
options: The particle is moving left at increasing speed.
The particle is moving left at decreasing speed.
The particle is moving right at decreasing speed.
The particle is moving right at increasing speed.
questions.hint: The sign of \(v\) gives the direction; compare the sign of \(v\) with the sign of the gradient (acceleration).

steps.explain: At \(P\) the graph is BELOW the axis: \(v<0\), so the particle moves LEFT.
The graph is rising at \(P\) (positive gradient): \(a>0\).
Velocity negative and acceleration positive act in opposite directions, so the speed is DECREASING.

keyPoints.text: describes the motion
keyPoints.note: Velocity and acceleration with opposite signs mean slowing down.

questions.stem: A boat has velocity \(v(t)=\dfrac{100}{(t+2)^2}\) metres per second at time \(t\) seconds after its engine is turned off. Show that the acceleration on the boat is always oppositely directed to its motion.
questions.answer: a = dv/dt = −200(t + 2)⁻³ = −200/(t + 2)³ < 0 for all t ≥ 0, while v > 0. Velocity is positive and acceleration is negative, so the acceleration is always opposite to the motion.
questions.hint: Differentiate the velocity to get the acceleration and compare the signs of \(a\) and \(v\).

steps.explain: Write \(v\) as a power.
Differentiate.
For \(t\geq0\), \((t+2)^3>0\) so \(a<0\) always; but \(v>0\) always.
Velocity is positive (forward) while the acceleration is negative (backward): they always point in opposite directions. ✓

keyPoints.text: Show that

questions.stem: A swimming pool is to be emptied for maintenance. The quantity of water, \(Q\) litres, remaining in the pool at a time, \(t\) minutes after it starts to drain, is given by \(Q(t)=2000(25-t)^{2},\ t\ge 0\). At what time does the rate of flow of water from the pool reach \(20\,000\) L/minute?
questions.hint: The rate of change of the quantity is \(Q'(t)\). Water is LEAVING the pool, so a flow of 20 000 L/min out means \(Q'(t)=-20\,000\).

steps.explain: The rate at which the quantity changes is the derivative \(Q'(t)\). Use the chain rule: derivative of \((25-t)^{2}\) is \(2(25-t)\times(-1)\).
Water is flowing OUT of the pool, so the quantity is DEcreasing and \(Q'(t)\) is negative. A flow of 20 000 L/min out means \(Q'(t)=-20\,000\) (orange level on the graph).

questions.stem: The displacement of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the equation \(x=2t-\dfrac{1}{2}t^{2}\), where \(x\) is in metres, \(t\) is in seconds and \(t\ge0\). Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: The particle is initially moving to the left.
The particle is at the origin after 4 seconds.
The acceleration of the particle is constant.
The speed of the particle increases indefinitely.
questions.hint: Find velocity \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}\) and acceleration \(a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\). Then test each statement: initial velocity (sign gives the direction), \(x\) at \(t=4\), the form of \(a\), and the behaviour of \(|v|\) as \(t\to\infty\).

steps.explain: Differentiate.
A: initially (\(t=0\)): \(v=2-0=2>0\). A positive velocity means moving to the RIGHT (the orange start of the graph rises). So 'moving to the left' is FALSE.
B: \(t=4\): \(x=2(4)-\dfrac{1}{2}(16)=8-8=0\): at the origin. TRUE (red point).
C: \(a=-1\) m s\(^{-2}\) never changes: constant. TRUE.
D: \(v=2-t\) gets more and more negative, so \(|v|=|2-t|\to\infty\): the speed increases without limit. TRUE.
The FALSE statement is A.
So the correct choice is option A.

options: \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=e^{t}-6e^{2t}=e^{t}\left(1-6e^{t}\right)\). \(v=0\) only when \(e^{t}=\dfrac{1}{6}\), i.e. \(t=\ln\dfrac{1}{6}\approx-1.79<0\), which is outside \(t\geq0\), so \(v\) is never 0
\(v=e^{t}-6e^{2t}\) can never be 0 because \(e^{t}\) is always positive, so each term is positive
\(x=e^{t}-3e^{2t}\) is never 0 for \(t\geq0\), so the particle is never at rest
The acceleration \(a=e^{t}-12e^{2t}\) is never 0 for \(t\geq0\), so the particle never stops
questions.hint: At rest means VELOCITY \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0\) (not the position or acceleration). Differentiate, factorise, solve \(v=0\), and then check whether the solution is allowed (\(t\geq0\)). Merely saying '\(e^{t}\) is never 0' is not enough.

steps.explain: At rest means \(v=0\). Find the velocity by differentiating the displacement.
Factorise (take out \(e^{t}\)).
Solve \(v=0\): \(e^{t}\) is never 0, so the bracket must be 0.
This time is NEGATIVE, but the motion only exists for \(t\geq0\). So there is no allowed time with \(v=0\): the velocity stays negative (\(v(0)=1-6=-5\)) and the particle never comes to rest.

Why not the others: B is false (the terms \(e^{t}\) and \(-6e^{2t}\) have different signs, so they CAN cancel); C confuses position with velocity; D uses acceleration, which is irrelevant to being at rest.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: A particle \(P_1\) has acceleration \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = e^{-t}+e^{-2t}\) (in m/s\(^2\)). Initially, \(P_1\) is \(\dfrac34\) m to the right of the origin, travelling at velocity \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac32\) m/s.

parts.stem: (a) Show that the displacement of the particle is given by \(x = e^{-t}+\dfrac14 e^{-2t}-\dfrac12\).

steps.explain: Integrate the acceleration once to find velocity, including a constant \(C_1\).
Use the initial condition \(\dot x(0) = -\tfrac32\) to solve for \(C_1\).
Integrate velocity once more to find displacement, including a constant \(C_2\).
Use the initial condition \(x(0)=\tfrac34\) to solve for \(C_2\).
Write the final displacement equation.

parts.stem: (b) Find the limiting displacement of \(P_1\), and hence state the limiting distance that \(P_1\) travels.
options: Limiting displacement \(=\dfrac34\) m; limiting distance travelled \(=\dfrac34\) m
Limiting displacement \(=-\dfrac12\) m; limiting distance travelled \(=\dfrac14\) m
Limiting displacement \(=-\dfrac12\) m; limiting distance travelled \(=1\dfrac14\) m
Limiting displacement \(=0\) m; limiting distance travelled \(=\dfrac12\) m
parts.hint: As \(t\to\infty\), both \(e^{-t}\) and \(e^{-2t}\) approach 0. The particle starts at \(\tfrac34\) and moves to this limiting position — the distance travelled is the size of that gap.

steps.explain: As \(t\to\infty\), both exponential terms decay to 0.
Substitute these limits into the displacement equation from part (a).

The particle starts at \(x=\tfrac34\) m (to the right of the origin) and moves steadily to \(x=-\tfrac12\) m (to the left of the origin) as \(t\to\infty\) — since it never reverses direction (velocity stays negative throughout, as \(-e^{-t}-\tfrac12e^{-2t}<0\) always), the total distance travelled is simply the size of this displacement change.

parts.stem: (c) A second particle \(P_2\) moves simultaneously, with acceleration \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -e^{-t}-e^{-2t}\). It is also \(\dfrac34\) m to the right of the origin, travelling at velocity \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac32\) m/s, when \(t=\ln3\) seconds. Write P₁'s velocity (from part a's working) and \(P_2\)'s velocity, then set them equal to find when the two particles share the same velocity.
Set the two velocities equal and collect all terms on one side.
This is quadratic in \(e^{-t}\). Multiply through by 9 to clear the fraction, then apply the quadratic formula with \(u=e^{-t}\).

Take the natural logarithm of both sides and solve for \(t\) (leaving the answer unsimplified, as instructed).

questions.stem: A particle is moving along the x-axis. The graph shows the velocity, \(v\) m/s, of the particle as a function of time, \(t\) seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin. The velocity is \(v(t)=4t-t^2\) for \(0\le t\le5\) and \(v(t)=-5\) for \(t>5\).

parts.stem: At what time will the particle return to the origin? Leave your answer in fraction form.
parts.hint: The displacement from the origin is the total signed area under the velocity graph, \(x(T) = \int_0^T v(t)\,dt\). The particle returns to the origin when its net displacement equals zero.

keyPoints.text: At what time will the particle return to the origin? Leave your answer in fraction form.
keyPoints.note: Identify the given information in this exact phrase first, then connect it to the rule or calculation shown in the solution.

steps.explain:
Returning to the origin means the particle's total displacement is zero:
\[x(T) = x(0) + \int_0^T v(t)\,dt = 0\]
On a velocity–time graph, displacement is represented by the **net signed area** between the curve and the \(t\)-axis:
- For \(0 \le t \le 4\), \(v(t) \ge 0\): the particle moves in the positive direction (positive area, \(\Delta x \gt 0\)).
- For \(t \gt 4\), \(v(t) \lt 0\): the particle reverses and moves backwards toward the origin (negative area, \(\Delta x \lt 0\)).

Therefore, the particle first returns to the origin when the area accumulated below the \(t\)-axis cancels the area above the \(t\)-axis.

parts.stem: When is the acceleration of the particle zero?
parts.hint: Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph, \(a(t) = v'(t)\). Find where the slope of the velocity graph is zero on each interval.

keyPoints.text: When is the acceleration of the particle zero?
keyPoints.note: Identify the given information in this exact phrase first, then connect it to the rule or calculation shown in the solution.

steps.explain:
Acceleration is the derivative (gradient) of velocity: \(a(t) = v'(t)\).

For \(0 \le t \lt 5\), the velocity is quadratic. Differentiating with respect to time gives:
\[a(t) = \dfrac{d}{dt}(4t - t^2) = 4 - 2t\]
Set this equal to zero to find when acceleration is zero:
\[4 - 2t = 0 \implies 2t = 4 \implies t = 2\text{ s}\]
This corresponds to the vertex (horizontal tangent) of the parabola at \((2, 4)\).

For \(t \gt 5\), the velocity is constant: \(v(t) = -5\).

The derivative of any constant function is zero:
\[a(t) = \dfrac{d}{dt}(-5) = 0\quad \text{for all } t \gt 5\]
On the graph, this corresponds to the horizontal line segment where the gradient is zero.

Examine the transition point at \(t = 5\):
- Left-hand gradient: \(\lim_{t \to 5^-} v'(t) = 4 - 2(5) = -6\)
- Right-hand gradient: \(\lim_{t \to 5^+} v'(t) = 0\)

Because the left and right gradients differ, the graph has a sharp corner at \(t = 5\), so the acceleration is undefined at \(t = 5\).

Combining the valid intervals, the acceleration is zero when:
\[\boxed{t = 2\text{ or }t \gt 5}\]

questions.stem: A boat travelling in a straight line in a still lake has its engine turned off at time \(t=0\) seconds. Its velocity \(v\) metres per second at time \(t\) seconds thereafter is given by \(v(t)=\dfrac{100}{(t+2)^2}\). Discuss \(v(t)\) as \(t\to\infty\) and hence the motion of the boat.
options: The velocity tends to 0 but never reaches it: the boat slows down and gets closer to rest, but never stops completely
The velocity tends to infinity: the boat speeds up forever
The velocity becomes 0 at \(t=2\): the boat stops after 2 seconds
The velocity becomes negative: the boat reverses direction
questions.hint: Look at what happens to \(\dfrac{100}{(t+2)^2}\) when the bottom becomes very large.

steps.explain: As \(t\to\infty\), \((t+2)^2\to\infty\).
But \(v(t)>0\) for every \(t\) (a positive number divided by a positive number), so \(v\) never equals 0 and never becomes negative.
The boat keeps moving forward ever more slowly, approaching rest but never stopping → A

keyPoints.text: Discuss
keyPoints.note: v → 0 as t → ∞ but v is always positive.

steps.explain: First stretch: the curve lies ON the axis for the whole interval from 0 to \(t_{1}\), so the particle is at rest for ALL times \(0\le t\le t_{1}\) (an interval, not just the single time \(t_{1}\)).
Second point: the curve crosses the \(t\)-axis at \(t_{3}\) (it changes from positive to negative velocity), so \(v=0\) at the single instant \(t=t_{3}\).

The other labelled times are not at rest: at \(t_{2}\) the velocity is at its MAXIMUM (fastest), and at \(t_{4}\) the velocity is negative (moving left). Note \(t_{1}\) alone is not the answer because the particle is at rest for all of \([0,t_{1}]\).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: When is the particle at rest?
keyPoints.note: At rest means velocity zero: a flat stretch on the axis counts as a whole interval.

questions.stem: A particle moves in a straight line and is initially 10 metres right of the origin. The velocity-time graph shown describes this motion. When is the particle farthest to the right of the origin?
questions.hint: The particle moves right while \(v>0\) and left while \(v<0\). It is farthest right at the moment \(v\) changes from positive to negative.

steps.explain: Where \(v>0\) (green) the particle moves to the right, so its displacement increases. Where \(v<0\) (red) it moves to the left, so its displacement decreases.
The velocity is positive from just after \(t_{1}\) until it crosses the axis at \(t_{3}\), then negative. So \(x\) increases until \(t_{3}\) and decreases after it.
steps.work: \(x\ \text{has a maximum where }v\text{ changes from + to −: }t=t_{3}\)

steps.explain: At \(t_{3}\) the particle turns round at its largest displacement. \(t_{2}\) is when velocity (not position) is largest, which is a different thing (option C).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.text: When is the particle farthest to the right of the origin?
keyPoints.note: Farthest right is where velocity changes from positive to negative, not where velocity is largest.

steps.explain: Starting point: the particle is initially 10 m right of the origin, so \(x(0)=10\). The graph starts at height 10 (not at 0).
From 0 to \(t_{1}\): \(v=0\), so the gradient of \(x(t)\) is 0: a flat horizontal line at \(x=10\) (green dashed).

From \(t_{1}\) to \(t_{3}\): \(v>0\), so \(x\) increases. The gradient \(v\) rises to a maximum at \(t_{2}\), so the graph gets steeper up to \(t_{2}\) (concave up) and less steep after (concave down): an INFLECTION point at \(t_{2}\) (orange).
At \(t_{3}\): \(v=0\) and changes from positive to negative, so \(x'=0\) there and \(x\) switches from increasing to decreasing: a MAXIMUM turning point at \(t_{3}\) (red).

After \(t_{3}\): \(v<0\), so \(x\) decreases, getting steeper (the velocity gets more negative), and may cross the \(t\)-axis as the particle passes the origin. Putting these features together gives the graph below.

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. After time \(t\) seconds its displacement \(x\) metres from a fixed point \(O\) on the line is given by \(x=t-3\ln(t+1)\). The particle returns to its starting point after \(T\) seconds. Find when the particle is at rest.
questions.hint: At rest means the velocity is zero. Velocity is the derivative of displacement: \(v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}\).

steps.explain: Differentiate \(x=t-3\ln(t+1)\): the derivative of \(\ln(t+1)\) is \(\dfrac{1}{t+1}\).
At rest: \(v=0\).
Multiply by \(t+1\), then subtract 1.
On the graph this is the lowest point, where the tangent is flat (red point). Check: \(v(2)=1-\dfrac{3}{3}=0\) ✓.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. After time \(t\) seconds its displacement \(x\) metres from a fixed point \(O\) on the line is given by \(x=t-3\ln(t+1)\). The particle returns to its starting point after \(T\) seconds. Find in simplest exact form, the distance travelled by the particle in the first \(T\) seconds of its motion.
questions.hint: Distance is not displacement. The particle starts at \(O\), goes one way until it stops at \(t=2\), then returns to \(O\) at \(t=T\). Total distance \(=\) distance out \(+\) distance back \(=2\times\) (the distance out).

steps.explain: Start: \(x(0)=0-3\ln1=0\), so the particle starts at \(O\). It is at rest at \(t=2\) (turning point, from part (a)).
Position at the turning point: \(x(2)=2-3\ln3\approx-1.30\) (negative, so it is 1.30 m on the other side of \(O\)).
Distance out \(=|x(2)-x(0)|=|2-3\ln3|=3\ln3-2\) (since \(3\ln3\approx3.30>2\)).
The particle then returns to its starting point \(O\) at \(t=T\), covering the same distance back (purple). It never turns again, so the total distance is twice the distance out.
Option B is only the distance out; option C is the (negative) displacement at \(t=2\).

questions.stem: The population of an ant colony is modelled by \( P=1000e^{kt} \), where \( t \) is measured in weeks.

parts.stem: (a) Find the initial population (at \( t=0 \)).

steps.explain: The initial population occurs at \( t=0 \). Substitute this into the model.
Any number to the power 0 equals 1.

parts.stem: (b) After 5 weeks the population is 15 000. Find the exact expression and the value of \( k \), correct to 4 decimal places.

steps.explain: Substitute \( t=5 \) and \( P=15\,000 \) into the model \( P=1000e^{kt} \).
Divide both sides by 1000 to isolate the exponential term.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to bring \( k \) out of the exponent.
Divide both sides by 5, then evaluate \( \ln15\approx2.7081 \).

parts.stem: (c) Using \( k=0.5416 \) from part (b), during which week will the population first exceed 50 000?

steps.explain: Set up the inequality for the population exceeding 50 000, using \( k=0.5416 \).
Divide both sides by 1000.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to bring \( t \) out of the exponent.
Divide both sides by 0.5416, then evaluate.
Since \( t\approx7.22 \) weeks is between week 7 and week 8, the population first exceeds 50 000 during the 8th week.
Part (a): the initial population is found by substituting \(t=0\) into the model \(P=1000e^{kt}\).
Part (b): use the condition that at \(t=5\) weeks, the population is 15000, and substitute into the model.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to solve for \(k\).
Evaluate to 4 decimal places, confirming the given value.
Part (c): find when the population first exceeds 50000 by substituting \(P=50000\) into the model and solving for t.
steps.work: \(50000 = 1000e^{0.5416t}\)\\ \(50 = e^{0.5416t}\)\\ \(\ln(50) = 0.5416t\)\\ \(t = \dfrac{\ln(50)}{0.5416} \approx \dfrac{3.912}{0.5416} \approx 7.22\text{ weeks}\)\\ Since \(t \approx 7.22\) falls after the end of week 7 (i.e. during the 8th week of growth), the population first exceeds 50000 during week 8.

questions.stem: The population \(P\) of a certain bird is decreasing at a rate proportional to \(P\). That is \(\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-kP\), where \(k\) is a positive integer and \(t\) is measured in years. In January 2010, there were 5000 birds and by January 2020, the population had decreased to 3450. If the population continues to decrease at this rate, what will be the expected population in 2030?
questions.hint: Decay model: \(P=P_{0}e^{-kt}\). Use 2010 to 2020 (\(t=10\)) to find \(k\), then evaluate at \(t=20\) (2030).

steps.explain: Solving \(\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-kP\) gives \(P=P_{0}e^{-kt}\) with \(P_{0}=5000\) (the 2010 population, \(t=0\)).
In 2020, \(t=10\) and \(P=3450\). Substitute and divide by 5000.
Take natural logs to find \(k\) (note: \(k\approx0.037\) is not an integer; the stem's wording does not affect the calculation).
In 2030, \(t=20\). Use \(e^{-20k}=\left(e^{-10k}\right)^{2}=0.69^{2}\) (no rounding needed).
Calculate.
Option B subtracts the same drop (1550) again (a straight-line model, not exponential); option C multiplies by 0.6.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: A radioactive substance is decaying and releasing radiation. The amount of radiation \(R\) at time \(t\), in years, is given by \(R=R_{0}e^{-2.89\times10^{-5}t}\) where \(R_{0}\) is the initial amount of radiation. Calculate the half-life of the substance, to the nearest 10 years.
questions.hint: Half-life is the time for the amount to fall to half: put \(R=\dfrac{1}{2}R_{0}\), divide by \(R_{0}\), then take natural logs.

steps.explain: Half the initial amount means \(R=\dfrac{1}{2}R_{0}\).
Divide both sides by \(R_{0}\) (it cancels, so the answer does not depend on the starting amount).
Take the natural log of both sides (\(\ln e^{x}=x\)).
Divide by \(-2.89\times10^{-5}\). \(\ln\dfrac{1}{2}=-0.6931\), so the negatives cancel.
Round to the nearest 10 years.
Option B is \(\dfrac{1}{2.89\times10^{-5}}\) (it forgets the \(\ln\dfrac{1}{2}\)); option C uses \(\log_{10}\) instead of \(\ln\).
So the correct choice is option A.
